    """Existing implementation: tests report missed alerts and duplicate ids."""

title: Count HTTP outcomes
prompt: Summarize normalized access-log records for an incident report. Count records in each HTTP status class.
constraints: Each record has integer status from 100 to 599. Return only observed classes as string keys such as "2xx".
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Integer division maps a status to its class.
A dictionary can count each class in one pass.
explanation: Aggregate by status // 100. Empty input produces an empty mapping; missing traffic is not a healthy percentage.
complexity: O(n) time; at most five counters.
followUp: What additional information would distinguish no traffic from missing telemetry?

title: Rank services by failures
prompt: Prioritize an incident by counting server errors per service. Rank the services with errors.
constraints: Records have service (string) and status (integer). Count statuses 500–599 only. Return service names by count descending, then name ascending for ties.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Filter before counting.
Use a tuple sort key: negative count, then name.
explanation: Count customer-visible server errors and sort the aggregated keys. This ranks volume, not error ratio.
complexity: O(n + s log s) time, O(s) space.
followUp: Why might a low-traffic service with 100% failures rank below a healthier busy service?

title: Compute a nearest-rank percentile
prompt: Calculate a tail-latency statistic from a bounded batch of raw millisecond measurements.
constraints: Values are nonnegative numbers; 0 < p <= 100. Return sorted[ceil(p*n/100)-1]. Return None for no samples.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Sort a copy, not the input list.
Nearest rank uses ceiling, then a zero-based index.
explanation: The explicit nearest-rank convention matters: different percentile definitions produce different answers for small samples.
complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
followUp: Why does a histogram-derived p95 differ from an exact percentile of raw samples?

title: Count failures in a rolling window
prompt: Implement the event selection behind a rolling error counter.
constraints: Events contain timestamp (integer seconds) and status. Count 500–599 when now-window < timestamp <= now. Events may be unsorted. window is positive.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Write both window boundaries before the loop.
Exclude future events as well as old events.
explanation: A half-open boundary avoids counting an event twice at adjoining interval edges. Future telemetry must not enter the current window.
complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
followUp: How would you update this efficiently for a timestamp-sorted continuous stream?
solution:
def window_errors(events, now, window):
    return sum(1 for event in events if now - window < event["timestamp"] <= now and 500 <= event["status"] <= 599)

title: Calculate remaining error budget
prompt: Report how many additional failed requests fit into a request-based error budget.
constraints: total and failures are nonnegative integers; failures <= total. slo_bps is 0–10000 basis points. Allowed failures = floor(total*(10000-slo_bps)/10000). Return allowed minus failures, including negative values.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Keep the computation in integers to avoid floating point drift.
Negative budget is useful evidence; do not clamp it.
explanation: Basis points make the contract exact. Integer floor prevents promising a fractional failed request.
complexity: O(1) time and space.
followUp: Why does a request-based budget differ from a time-based availability budget?
solution:
def remaining_budget(total, failures, slo_bps):
    return total * (10000 - slo_bps) // 10000 - failures

title: Find missing heartbeat intervals
prompt: Find gaps in scheduled heartbeat timestamps so an operator can inspect missing telemetry.
constraints: start <= end; interval > 0; all values are integer seconds. Return missing scheduled times start, start+interval, ... <= end. Duplicate or off-schedule timestamps do not create extra slots.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Build a set of received timestamps.
Generate the schedule independently of observed values.
explanation: Comparing with an expected schedule detects absence. Only looking at received events cannot identify all missing data.
complexity: O(n + k) time, O(n + k) space for n events and k slots.
followUp: How would clock skew change the definition of a missed heartbeat?

title: Generate capped retry delays
prompt: Prepare a deterministic exponential-backoff schedule. This function computes delays; it does not sleep or send requests.
constraints: attempts, base_ms and cap_ms are nonnegative integers. Attempt zero waits min(base_ms, cap_ms); each later delay doubles until capped. Return one delay per retry.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Carry the capped delay forward.
Zero attempts produces no retry.
explanation: Capping before the next iteration avoids ever-growing integers. Production clients also need jitter, a retry budget and an overall deadline.
complexity: O(attempts) time and output space.
followUp: When would retrying a failed request be unsafe even with backoff?
solution:
def retry_delays(attempts, base_ms, cap_ms):
    delays = []
    delay = min(base_ms, cap_ms)
    for _ in range(attempts):
        delays.append(delay)
        delay = min(delay * 2, cap_ms)
    return delays

title: Implement a token bucket
prompt: Decide whether each timestamped request is admitted by a per-process token bucket.
constraints: Timestamps are nonnegative seconds in nondecreasing order. capacity is a positive integer; refill_per_second is nonnegative. Start full at time 0. Refill to capacity before each request; admitting consumes one token. Return booleans.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Track both tokens and last observed time.
Rejected requests do not consume tokens; simultaneous requests do not refill.
explanation: A bucket permits a burst up to capacity while limiting long-run rate. Refill is based on elapsed time, even after a rejected request.
complexity: O(n) time; O(1) state excluding output.
followUp: How would you coordinate this policy across multiple API replicas?
solution:
def admit_requests(timestamps, capacity, refill_per_second):
    tokens, previous = capacity, 0
    result = []
    for timestamp in timestamps:
        tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (timestamp - previous) * refill_per_second)
        allowed = tokens >= 1
        result.append(allowed)
        if allowed:
            tokens -= 1
        previous = timestamp
    return result

title: Find the circuit-opening event
prompt: Locate the first point at which consecutive failures would open a simplified circuit breaker.
constraints: outcomes contains booleans: True is success, False is failure. threshold is a positive integer. Return the zero-based index of the first threshold-length failure streak, or None. Success resets the streak.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: A total failure count is not a consecutive streak.
Reset state on each success.
explanation: A consecutive-failure policy is a simplified breaker trigger. A real breaker also needs an open duration and half-open probes.
complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
followUp: When might a rolling error ratio be a better trigger than consecutive failures?

title: Merge maintenance windows
prompt: Combine overlapping or touching maintenance windows into a minimal list for a status page.
constraints: Each window is [start, end] with start <= end. Input may be unsorted. Touching windows merge. Return merged windows in ascending start order.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Sort a copy by start.
Compare each interval to the end of the current merged interval.
explanation: The invariant is that finished intervals cannot overlap any remaining interval. Copy interval values so extending a result does not mutate input.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
followUp: Would touching windows still merge if they belonged to different services?

title: Order service startup safely
prompt: Plan startup for services whose dependencies must be ready first. Detect cycles rather than waiting forever.
constraints: Input maps every service name to a list of dependency names; every dependency is also a key. Lists have no duplicates. Choose the lexicographically smallest currently ready service at each step. Return None if there is a cycle.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Track outstanding dependency counts and reverse edges.
A min-heap makes the ready-service tie-break explicit.
If fewer than all services are emitted, a cycle remains.
explanation: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes a ready vertex. Counting all emitted vertices detects cycles even when a different component can start.
complexity: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space.
followUp: How would you distinguish a dependency cycle from a service that is merely slow to become ready?

title: Measure peak in-flight work
prompt: Estimate the maximum simultaneously active requests from completed request intervals.
constraints: Each interval is [start, end) with start <= end. Zero-length intervals count as no work. An end at time t is processed before a start at t. Return the maximum active count.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Convert intervals into start and end events.
Sort end events before starts at equal timestamps.
explanation: The half-open convention matters at ties. Ignoring zero-length work prevents negative counts from isolated equal-time events.
complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
followUp: Why is peak concurrency insufficient to determine a sustainable worker-pool size?

title: Detect configuration drift
prompt: Compare two flat configuration maps before reconciling a service.
constraints: Return sorted keys that are missing on either side or have unequal JSON scalar values. Missing is different from a present None. Values have consistent types when a key exists in both maps.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Inspect the union of keys.
Use membership checks before comparing values.
explanation: A default of None conflates absence with an explicit null. Membership captures the operational distinction.
complexity: O(k log k) time, O(k) space.
followUp: Which configuration fields should be ignored because a controller owns them?
solution:
def config_drift(desired, actual):
    return sorted(key for key in desired.keys() | actual.keys() if key not in desired or key not in actual or desired[key] != actual[key])

title: Deduplicate webhook deliveries
prompt: Keep the first delivery of each incident event so repeated webhook delivery does not duplicate notifications.
constraints: Each event has a string id and arbitrary JSON fields. Return complete first-seen records in input order. Later copies of an id are ignored even if their payload differs.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Track IDs separately from output records.
Do not sort: first delivery determines output order.
explanation: An idempotency key defines duplicate identity. This in-memory implementation is a batch exercise; production needs durable state and retention.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
followUp: What happens if a process crashes after sending a notification but before saving the idempotency key?

title: Route integer keys to shards
prompt: Build a deterministic modulo router for a batch of integer tenant IDs.
constraints: shard_count is positive; keys are nonnegative integers. Return a mapping with string shard indexes for nonempty shards only. Assign key % shard_count and preserve key order within each shard. Keep duplicates.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Modulo gives an index in the target range.
Do not use process-randomized hash values for an integer ID.
explanation: Modulo routing is simple and deterministic. Changing the shard count moves many keys; this is deliberately not consistent hashing.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
followUp: How would rendezvous hashing reduce movement when a shard is added?

title: Plan bounded rollout batches
prompt: Split an ordered host list into rollout waves without exceeding the specified batch size.
constraints: batch_size is a positive integer. Preserve order and duplicates. Every batch except the last must contain batch_size hosts. Empty input returns an empty list.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Advance the index by batch_size.
A slice naturally handles the final partial batch.
explanation: Batching bounds simultaneous changes, but healthy gates between waves are still required before this becomes a safe deployment workflow.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
followUp: What evidence would make you pause before starting the next batch?
solution:
def rollout_batches(hosts, batch_size):
    return [hosts[index:index + batch_size] for index in range(0, len(hosts), batch_size)]

title: Identify disk-pressure candidates
prompt: Evaluate normalized disk usage without dividing by an unknown capacity.
constraints: Each disk has name, used and capacity (nonnegative integers). threshold_percent is 0–100. Include disks with positive capacity and used/capacity*100 >= threshold. Preserve input order. Zero capacity is unknown and excluded.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Check capacity before comparing utilization.
Cross multiplication avoids division and rounding.
explanation: An exact integer comparison treats the boundary correctly. Unknown capacity requires a separate telemetry check rather than a fabricated utilization.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
followUp: Which other signals would distinguish nearly full storage from an imminent outage?
solution:
def pressured_disks(disks, threshold_percent):
    return [disk["name"] for disk in disks if disk["capacity"] > 0 and disk["used"] * 100 >= threshold_percent * disk["capacity"]]

title: Redact structured log secrets
prompt: Remove sensitive values from nested JSON logs before exporting them to an observability backend.
constraints: Recursively handle dictionaries, lists and JSON scalars. Replace values of case-insensitive keys password, token and authorization with "[REDACTED]". Preserve key spelling and all other values. Input keys are strings.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Handle mappings, sequences and scalar values separately.
Redact a sensitive key before recursing into its value.
explanation: Build new containers recursively. This policy is intentionally explicit; it does not detect secrets embedded in arbitrary free text.
complexity: O(n) time and space for all visited values; O(depth) recursion stack.
followUp: How would you test this policy against newly introduced credential fields without logging the credentials?
